title: The Quest to End Hangovers
author: @NewYorker
content:
A few months ago, while watching Instagram stories, I came across a provocative advertisement. A man with scruffy brown hair said, “What if I told you alcohol is not actually bad for you?” He explained that our livers convert alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic molecule that he described as a main cause of hangovers. His brief chemistry lesson, which used glass beakers filled with colorful liquids as props, was accompanied by a link to a product: a supplement that promised to neutralize acetaldehyde more quickly than my body could on its own. Eliminating acetaldehyde, the ad claimed, would help conquer hangovers. One reviewer of the supplement said that she’d drunk more than five glasses of wine and felt fine the next day.

I usually have a strong aversion to the science-y veneer of supplement marketing, yet I stuck with the ad to the end. I like drinking; I learned about fine wine while working in restaurants, and I still enjoy pairing a carefully selected bottle with dinner. My favorite cocktail, the Perfect Manhattan, is basically all booze: rye whiskey, sweet vermouth, and dry vermouth, plus bitters and a brandied cherry. But as I entered my thirties, hangovers became more menacing—I began limiting my drinks and gulping well-timed waters—and I grew concerned about the health effects of drinking. Somehow, I’d never heard of acetaldehyde.

After I watched the ad, more purported hangover remedies flooded my Instagram feed. I scrolled through them with detached curiosity, occasionally clicking on a link, and this, of course, unleashed even more ads. There were many different products, with various ingredients, but they all seemed to tell the same story—that they could vanquish hangovers by counteracting acetaldehyde. Some, with peppy names like Cheers, Drinking Buddies, and No Days Wasted, highlighted dihydromyricetin, more commonly known as DHM, a flavonoid, derived from East Asian plants, which had been tested in mice. One company, ZBiotics, touts a bacteria modified to produce an enzyme that breaks acetaldehyde down. Another was marketing an amino acid that also purportedly processed acetaldehyde. The ads made it sound like a sort of morning-after pill for drinking had just been discovered. Could it really be so simple?

Scientists have known about acetaldehyde for decades, and it’s widely agreed that the compound—a known carcinogen—can make us feel sick. As Howard Edenberg, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the Indiana University School of Medicine, explained to me, when we drink alcohol a group of enzymes called alcohol dehydrogenases, or ADHs, convert it into acetaldehyde. But, under normal circumstances, the metabolic journey of alcohol doesn’t end there. A family of enzymes called aldehyde dehydrogenases, or ALDHs, soon turn it into a harmless molecule called acetate.

Sometimes our body’s machinery for processing alcohol falters in instructive ways. In the nineties, Edenberg helped identify genetic differences linked to overactive ADH enzymes, which would cause people to turn alcohol into acetaldehyde more quickly. Another genetic variation reduces the effectiveness of ALDHs, meaning that the toxic acetaldehyde sticks around for longer than it should. People with this genetic variant often experience facial flushing (sometimes called “Asian glow” because it’s common among people of East Asian descent), or have a very hard time clearing out the acetaldehyde at all, leading to nausea after only small amounts of drinking.

Here the impact of acetaldehyde becomes messier than the supplement ads let on. Genetic deviations that impair the processing of alcohol turn out to be associated with lower rates of alcoholism. “My interpretation is that a buildup of acetaldehyde is, in fact, aversive,” Edenberg told me. In other words, spikes in acetaldehyde seem to nudge people to stop drinking. (Indeed, Antabuse, the first drug marketed for alcohol-use disorder, deliberately inhibits ALDHs, increasing acetaldehyde levels and making people feel ill when they drink.) Rodent experiments seem to back up this interpretation. When scientists decreased the rate at which acetaldehyde is processed in mice, they wound up drinking less alcohol. And when scientists helped the mice process acetaldehyde faster, “they continued drinking,” Yanina Pepino, a professor of ingestive behavior at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, told me.

New discoveries continue to be made about acetaldehyde. Although scientists long presumed that alcohol is converted to acetaldehyde in the liver, Pepino said that recent research in animals found that up to thirty per cent of acetaldehyde is transported over to the intestine through bile, and processed to acetate there instead—with unknown implications. Other scientists have noted that when alcohol reaches the brain, it is metabolized into acetaldehyde there; they wonder if, rather than make us feel bad, it can make us feel good. In animal models, the compound has been shown to bind with the neurotransmitter dopamine to activate the brain’s reward system.

The causes of hangovers are no less complicated. “It’s very simplistic to think that only acetaldehyde plays a major role,” Pepino told me. In people who produce normal ADHs and ALDHs, she said, there’s no evidence that acetaldehyde levels are linked to the severity of hangovers the next morning. Even if a connection exists, researchers would have a hard time documenting it. “Acetaldehyde is one of the most difficult molecules to measure that I have ever encountered,” Pepino said. On its own, the molecule doesn’t stay in the bloodstream for long. It’s highly reactive with many other molecules, so measuring its levels in the body is difficult. At room temperature it’s a gas, so in the laboratory it tends to vanish into the air.

So what causes a hangover, really? I was surprised to learn that scientists still don’t really know. Alcohol is a diuretic, so dehydration presumably plays a role—but rehydration isn’t enough to cure a hangover, so it can’t be the whole story. Jonathan Howland, an emeritus professor of emergency medicine at Boston University, who has studied hangovers and people who are mysteriously resistant to them, thinks that one possible source of the condition is methanol. The alcohol that generally makes a person feel drunk is ethanol, but adult beverages often contain small quantities of methanol, which build up while the ethanol is being processed by the body. He’s not certain enough to recommend any hangover deterrents, however. “Coming up with an intervention when you don’t know the mechanism in the first place is kind of dicey,” Howland told me.

Ignorance hasn’t discouraged humans from trying to stop hangovers in millennia past. One of the oldest known treatments, a string of shrubby leaves meant to be worn as a necklace, appeared in the text of a fraying piece of ancient Egyptian papyrus. Since then, raw egg yolks, pickle brine, cumin seeds, six-packs of Coke, and greasy breakfast sandwiches have all been credited with easing our post-drinking ailments. As Joan Acocella wrote for this magazine, in 2008, a suspicious number of cures happen to include alcohol as a main ingredient.

Some scientists speculate that acetaldehyde might trigger a release of the immune-signalling chemical histamine, leading to alcohol-intolerance symptoms. Pepino suspects that hangovers are the result of a broader immune response. Many classic signs of a hangover—headache, fatigue, nausea—also crop up when we have the flu. And it’s known that, after heavy drinking, markers of inflammation in the blood tend to spike, just as they do when we’re sick. “It’s so complex,” Pepino said. “That’s why we still don’t have a very crisp, clear grasp of what causes a hangover.”

Some of the ingredients found in hangover supplements are intriguing, Pepino told me. DHM is found naturally in Ampelopsis grossedentata, a Chinese vine tea, and in Hovenia dulcis, an East Asian fruit tree. Zhijuzi, as the seed of the tree is known in traditional Chinese medicine, appeared in China’s first pharmacopoeia, in the year 659; according to one folk saying, it was credited with keeping a person sober through “a thousand cups.” In rodent studies, DHM seemed to clear alcohol from the animals’ bodies, reduce liver damage, and alter alcohol’s effects on the brain. Scientists are now trying to develop DHM as a treatment for alcohol-use disorder.

The DHM supplements being marketed on social media have some problems, though. For one thing, they have not been studied clinically in humans. Instead, they’re being sold as dietary supplements, which means that companies don’t have to prove to the Food and Drug Administration that they work. For another, they come in a different form than the DHM used in the mouse studies. Scientists dissolved the DHM into a solution and then injected it into the gut, which meant that the mice could absorb most of it: fifty to seventy per cent of the compound was deemed “bioavailable.” Daryl Davies, a neuropharmacologist at U.S.C. who researches the compound, told me that in the capsules and powders sold online the bioavailability of DHM drops to five per cent—if you’re lucky.

Davies hopes to develop forms of DHM that are more bioavailable—but not necessarily for hangover treatments. Instead, he hopes that the compound might help people drink less. He and other researchers have gathered evidence that DHM interacts with receptors in the brain that make people feel relaxed and disinhibited; it may make alcohol feel less rewarding. If it helps the body metabolize alcohol, then it could also make drinking less fun. As a result, Davies thinks that the compound shows the most promise for serious alcohol-use disorder, or for people with liver damage—even if those conditions are less likely to inspire Instagram ads. “Of course, it’s easier to market it as a hangover remedy,” he said.

In June, I tried two DHM-based hangover supplements. Drinking Buddies is a liquid that claims to contain DHM along with an acetaldehyde-busting amino acid, herbs such as milk thistle, and B vitamins. I went to a dinner party and had several glasses of wine; when I got home, my husband and I debriefed at the kitchen table as we drank a sour cider together. For the sake of the experiment, I probably imbibed more than I normally would have. Then, as instructed, I took the supplement. When we woke up in the morning, my husband groaned. He said that his hangover was at full strength. I felt a little more clearheaded than him, but as the morning dragged on I felt a familiar lethargy and fatigue fall over me.

The second time, I tried Gush, a hangover product made from a Korean pear juice that was supposed to be naturally high in DHM. I tried not to change my drinking habits that evening: I drank only what I wanted, two glasses of wine at an early dinner, and I went to bed at a reasonable hour. When I woke up, I felt just fine. In both cases, I recognized a kind of karmic balance. I felt lousy in proportion to how much I’d drunk. Maybe no supplement was capable of changing that.

When I spoke to Davies, in mid-August, I happened to have a slight hangover once again. The day before had been my birthday, and I’d had several plastic cups of wine while lounging with friends in the park. Later, at a bar with a friend, I’d sipped a Manhattan while opening presents. As Davies talked about the effects of drinking, I experienced a tinge of guilt.

Still, I wasn’t sure that I wanted my hangover, or my guilt, to magically disappear. I pointed out to Davies that maybe the hangover was my body’s rightful revenge—a sort of checks-and-balances system that moderates our immoderation. Davies observed, however, that most of us aren’t very good at learning our lesson; by the next time your friends invite you for spritzes, the memory of suffering is likely to have faded.

Henry Jeffreys, the author of several books about drinking, including “Empire of Booze,” told me that there was something cosmically wrong about wanting to feel unaffected by a big night out. The drinking was the first act; the hangover the second. But Jessa Ramsay, an acquaintance of mine who works as a sales representative for a spiked coconut-water beverage , disagreed. She often feels that she has to drink as part of her job, and she wishes that she could dull its effects. For her, the dream of a hangover cure lives on. “In my mind, it’s like asking, Can you ever have joy without sadness?” she told me. “I think you absolutely can.” ♦

title: He Gave the Knicks Their Name. Why Was He Forgotten?
author: @NewYorker
content:
Mary Shelley, the author of “Frankenstein,” once developed a terrific little crush on Washington Irving, the author of “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.” This was in 1824, in London, and Shelley, twenty-seven, and two years the widow of Percy Bysshe Shelley, spent a season begging a mutual friend, the playwright and actor John Howard Payne, to set them up. Irving, just past forty, was a bona-fide influencer of the Romantic era—fêted on two continents, living in the highest style, surrounded “by fashion rank & splendid friendships,” as Shelley wrote to Payne in a letter. Shelley wrote Irving a series of notes, and gave them to Payne to deliver. Payne, who was apparently in love with Shelley himself, sat on them for a little while, but eventually relented. Irving swiped through the flirtations without a second glance. “Read Mrs. Shelley’s correspondence before going to bed,” the lifelong bachelor wrote in his diary.

Shelley gave up the pursuit soon after. “As to friendship with him—It cannot be,” she wrote to Payne. “Though every thing I hear & know renders it more desirable.” How could such a man, she sighed, “pilot his pleasure bark . . . into this sober, sad, enshadowed nook?”

Poor Payne. Irving was the first acknowledged master of American letters, the first man in the young Republic, it was said, to make a “profession” out of writing. Born in the closing days of the American Revolution, he helped define the years of America’s adolescence, pioneering forms such as the American essay, short story, and travelogue, as well as emergent genres like horror and the Western. By the end of his life, Irving had established himself as a respected biographer and a sometime international diplomat. (He served as Ambassador to Spain during the reign of Isabella II, and helped negotiate America’s remarkably sensible northern boundary with Canada.) In 1859, the year Irving died, the publication Home Journal declared him “by far the most honored man in our country”—and “curiously enough, even less honored than loved.”

Irving’s two masterpiece stories, “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” and “Rip Van Winkle,” were instant classics, told and retold until they were whittled down to folk tales, a form that Irving worshipped. The Headless Horseman still gallops through American imaginations today; “Rip Van Winkle,” in which a beleaguered upstate New York farmer falls asleep before the American Revolution and wakes up to find the world completely changed, has been adapted by the likes of H. G. Wells, Woody Allen, Octavia Butler, and Matt Groening. Irving coined the term “the almighty dollar,” helped establish the traditions of American Christmas (including the notion of St. Nicholas riding in a flying wagon), and popularized Gotham as New York City’s nickname. He bestowed on his beloved home town its first mascot, a fictional, crotchety old Dutch American historian named Diedrich Knickerbocker, whose legacy extends through this June’s N.B.A. championship. (Jalen Brunson, in his shaggy grace and undersized bullishness, has something of old Diedrich about him.)

When Irving was alive, everyone read him. “His Crayon, I know it by heart,” the usually acid Lord Byron wrote of Irving’s “The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.,” a collection stuffed with the shimmering blends of fact and fiction that Irving called “sketches.” Among his fans and friends were the First Lady Dolley Madison, Sir Walter Scott, and John Jacob Astor, New York City’s first multimillionaire. Scott, the preëminent Romantic-era novelist, took the younger Irving under his wing; Edgar Allan Poe, whose gothic tales owed much to Irving’s stories of goblins and will-o’-the-wisps, considered him a writer for whom “there is a vast deal to be said.” Some—including Poe—thought Irving overrated, in the way that best-selling writers are always overrated. Still, the title of Charles Dickens’s 1836 début, “Sketches by Boz,” was a nod to his once inescapable influence.

Today, of course, barely anyone reads Irving. Two decades ago, the essayist and longtime Columbia University writing professor Phillip Lopate was nosing through a cache of books being deaccessioned by the school’s library and found a complete set of Irving’s works, twelve volumes of about a thousand pages each. Not even Lopate, one of America’s foremost essayists and the editor of an anthology called “Writing New York,” had read much of him. He took the musty pile home more from pity than genuine interest, and they “sat on my own bookshelves collecting dust,” Lopate confesses at the start of “A Washington Irving Sketch Book: Reflections on an American Writer.” When Lopate finally brought himself to crack the books open, he was astonished to discover not an entombed literary mummy but a mirror—a writer whom Lopate came to think of as a long-lost literary doppelgänger. The resulting book, comprising some three dozen brisk, sketch-like chapters, is a reappraisal of Irving by an author who has come to see in him “the prototype of a writer’s life, with all its setbacks and triumphs”—particularly of a kind of New York City writer’s life.

The more he read, the more Lopate began to discover traces of Irving’s influence all around New York, and in himself. “I too was a bachelor,” Lopate, who in 1981 published an acclaimed collection titled “Bachelorhood: Tales of the Metropolis,” writes. He came to regard Irving as New York City’s original great bachelor, the Carrie Bradshaw of the city’s early gaslamp era. After an oncology checkup at the Weill-Cornell Medical Center and a lunch of pork fried rice in lower Manhattan, Lopate found himself wondering how a writer who was once the most celebrated American literary figure could wind up so forgotten. As the author of more than two dozen works of nonfiction, fiction, and poetry, Lopate began to consider what chance he has at posterity if someone like Irving can be lost. “I question the whole notion that this or that author no longer ‘speaks’ to us, no longer ‘matters,’ ” Lopate writes, speaking about Irving, and, perhaps, himself.

Irving was born in New York City on April 3, 1783, the son of a stern Scottish immigrant who ran a tidy import business selling wine, sugar, and hardware. The preliminary articles of the Treaty of Paris had been signed four months before, but it would be another seven months before the last British troops and warships left New York Harbor, marking the formal end of the War of Independence. The city was a mess. During the seven years that it was occupied by British forces, Manhattan had been ravaged by fires, picked over by looters, covered in fortifications, and swollen with refugees. Many New Yorkers who remained behind British lines during the war were not supporters of the Revolution, but in naming their son after George Washington, the Irvings declared their allegiance. According to family lore, the writer met his namesake in 1789, Washington’s first year as President, when his Scottish nanny, Lizzie, stopped the great man on a street in lower Manhattan. “There’s a bairn named after you,” she said. Washington placed his hand on Irving’s head, “little guessing that the boy would grow up to write his biography,” Lopate writes.

In his early twenties, Irving ran around town with a crew of nine well-to-do “blades” and cutups who called themselves the Lads of Kilkenny; the group included two of Irving’s elder brothers, the future congressman Gouverneur Kemble, and the future novelist James K. Paulding. The young men spent several summers together in an old mansion on the banks of the Passaic River, in New Jersey, “indulging in pranks, drinking orgies, and leapfrogging on the lawn.” Some have wondered whether Irving was gay, a speculation which Lopate dismisses, though he does quote from several suggestive letters to friends. “I am almost ashamed to say. . . . Marriage is the grave of bachelor intimacies,” Irving wrote to his friend, Henry Brevoort, Jr., after the latter got engaged.

Starting in 1807, the Lads collaborated on a short-lived magazine called Salmagundi, named after a sailor’s stew. “We invite all editors of newspapers and literary journals to praise us heartily in advance,” they declared in the first of what would be twenty issues, published sporadically. Salmagundi gently skewered New York City life and society, and specialized, Lopate says, “in the sort of worked-up nonsense that proved quite popular with audiences of the day, being neither solemn nor mean-spirited.” The wry, winking tone still legible in its pages was an early iteration of the urbane magazine voice that powered nineteenth-century publications such as Judge and Puck, as well as later ones like The New Yorker, New York, Spy, and Gawker. Salmagundi spoke to a desire to mythologize New York as it became a metropolis, an impulse shared by the authors of the portentous histories and guides being released by the city’s nascent publishing industry, which Irving decided to ridicule in a “bulging comic tome” inspired by Swift and Cervantes. Consulting the sparse records of the then nascent New-York Historical Society, Irving invented the narrator Knickerbocker, and stretched the bit for four hundred pages “with the garrulous energy of a young writer just discovering his full powers,” Lopate writes.

“A History of New York from the Beginning of the World to the End of the Dutch Dynasty,” published when Irving was twenty-six, was a sensation, the first best-seller in New York’s history. Mixing social and political satire with the scraps of information then known about Dutch New York, Irving created a set of founding myths for his home town, consciously modelled on the founding myths of the world’s great ancient cities, with a crooked real-estate deal in place of the trials of Theseus, or fratricidal twins raised by a wolf. In his telling, the Lenape agreed to sell Dutch colonists only as much land on Manhattan as could be covered by a man’s breeches. After the deal was struck, the Dutch produced a man, Winant Ten Broeck, whose prodigious undies unfolded and unfolded until they draped over the entire island. “The simple savages, whose ideas of a man’s nether garments had never expanded beyond the dimensions of a breech clout, stared with astonishment and dismay as they beheld this bulbous-bottomed burgher peeled like an onion,” Irving wrote.

Some historians have seethed at Irving for forever “muddying” the city’s sense of its own history; others have recognized that Irving was trying to transcend what Plutarch (another historian who loved to embellish) derided as the “so-called rules of chronology.” “Virgil he wasn’t, but New York could have done worse,” the late Mike Wallace and Edwin G. Burrows wrote of Irving in their totemic social history “Gotham: A History of New York City to 1898.” Lopate comes down on the side of the defenders, arguing that Irving on the page was giving New York City “a mythological dimension beyond what the historical record warrants, like Gabriel García Márquez’s Macondo.”

Even when everyone read him, Irving had his critics. By 1819, when he published the first section of “The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.,” a collection of tales of English and American country life written under yet another pseudonym, he had been living in England for four years, which would turn into a nearly two-decade hiatus from the U.S. Though “The Sketch Book” contained both “Sleepy Hollow” and “Rip Van Winkle,” Irving’s most beloved and enduring works, Lopate suggests that it was the beginning of his downfall. Some American readers, still smarting from the War of 1812, wondered whether Irving had gone soft on the English, and if maybe he was too precious, too genteel, to speak for America. It’s a critique that his biographer, Stanley T. Williams, would reproduce in a scathing 1935 volume—“Irving himself wearies us, mild-mannered, urbane, indecisive . . . and, at times, timid and dependent”—and that Lopate, a self-described belletrist, seems to take personally. “It was generally acknowledged by [reviewers] that he had an ability to infuse his prose with a beguiling tone, regardless of subject matter,” he writes.

Irving, Lopate tells us, was an “abolitionist at heart,” but throughout his long career he spoke out little against slavery. Even his best works contain grotesque depictions of Black people and Native Americans; “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” describes Black New Yorkers with “grinning rows of ivory from ear to ear,” watching their rich white neighbors enjoy a country-house party. As Irving got older, he dedicated himself to a series of surprisingly well-researched and open-minded biographies of Christopher Columbus, the Prophet Muhammad, and the Anglo-Irish “hack” writer Oliver Goldsmith. Lopate spends ten pages considering Irving’s most curious work, “The Alhambra,” a loving account of the old Moorish castle in Granada, Spain, where he had been invited to live for several months by a local governor, who was a fan of his work. Living in the castle was the event of Irving’s life. “Often have I trod in fancy the romantic halls of the Alhambra,” he wrote. “As I inhale the odor of the rose, and feel the influence of the balmy climate, I am almost tempted to fancy myself in the paradise of Mahomet.” For many American readers, Irving’s writing—laden as it is with Orientalist clichés—provided a rare encounter with Islam.

When Irving returned to New York City in 1832, he was “stunned” by the steamships in the harbor, the enormous new hotels, the striking fashions on the streets. He had become his own creation, Rip Van Winkle. A large formal dinner was held in his honor, where he was proclaimed “the Father of American Literature,” and he stammered through an awkward speech. From then on, he thought of himself as a real writer, collecting steady book profits and taking on tepid magazine assignments to help sustain his glamorous life style, which made even more readers sour on him. On this, Lopate is magnanimous: “What writer since then has not been inveigled into doing a bit of hack writing when the wolf was at the door?”

Irving did manage to cobble together enough of a pile to buy a small estate on the Hudson River, north of the city, not far from the climatic scene in “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow.” He called the property Sunnyside, and he departed from it for an extended period only once, in 1842, when President John Tyler appointed him Ambassador to Spain. When he returned, he sat down to his final work, a five-part biography of Washington, and completed it just a few months before he died. Lopate, one of the few people in the past century to make his way through all three volumes, admits that it’s a snoozer. “1,272 pages, my God!” he writes. Still, he praises Irving’s instinctual dislike of hagiography, and his ability to find the “warm, complicated human being under the Houdon marble statue.”

There’s a nice bronze bust of Irving in the southeast corner of Prospect Park, in Brooklyn, right next to the central loop. Thousands of walkers, joggers, and bikers pass him by every day. As Lopate looked for other interpretations of Irving, he came across a book called “Sojourners,” by Philip J. McFarland, published in 1979, a trippy attempt not so much to chronicle Irving as to reconstruct him and his social milieu of friends, fans, and patrons in America and Europe. By re-creating “the worlds through which the wanderer Irving moved,” McFarland wrote, “I have undertaken to reveal, more fully perhaps than would the writer of a conventional biography.” Lopate adopts some of McFarland’s conclusions about Irving’s work, including his idea that Rip Van Winkle remains the exemplar of the American Everyman “who is no longer able to find anyone who remembers him or can tell him who he is.” Lopate writes that throughout his entire life, Irving was preparing for his own oblivion; he would have been surprised to hear how his creations have endured. Knicks in six, for example? Couldn’t have done it without him. ♦

title: How a Cowboy Rides When the Range is on Fire
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
When Rhonda MacDonald put out a plea for help on Facebook, the cowboys answered. Wildfires have been ravaging British Columbia, Canada, this summer—and when a ranch is put under evacuation, it is no easy feat to round up 150 free‑roaming cattle. The MacDonald herd was roaming a vast, 100,000‑acre expanse of Crown rangeland above the ranch, and the people of most use were those on horseback. This exhilarating piece documents the people who came to help, and honors the skills and hard‑won knowledge needed to navigate treacherous, fire‑scarred terrain to save the herd and help a neighbour in crisis.

Before the riders headed up Mimenuh Mountain, Wayne MacDonald stood in front of a whiteboard with a red Sharpie and began drawing. Not a map, exactly. More like 50 years of memory. He sketched the ridges, draws and escape routes cattle would choose under pressure. There was one thing he kept returning to: the lack of escape routes. “As far as road, there’s one in and one out.” They knew there might come a moment when staying was no longer brave – it was reckless.

title: Worm Munch Matters
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
“Sound is a tangible way of connecting to aspects of nature that are hidden from humans. The deep ocean, the dark night, and now the dense earth beneath our feet,” writes Ella Browning. And you can hear underground for yourself in the fascinating recordings she includes in her essay on earthworm “munching.” In this emerging field of soil ecoacoustics, researchers—including Browning—are finding links between ecosystem recovery and the character of underground soundscapes. Healthy soil literally sounds different. This piece will change how you view the ground beneath your feet.

A core principle of ecoacoustics is that complexly noisy natural places are healthier natural places. This means that it’s not just the volume of noise, but the diversity of sound that indicates habitat health. The dawn chorus in an intact Bornean tropical forest is magical in its complexity, especially if you’re lucky to experience it mixed in with the whoops of a troop of gibbons swinging through overhead, as I was during a visit in 2019.

In contrast, cities are generally not ecologically healthy and, while they are incredibly noisy places, they are filled with the harsh, more monotonous sounds of car engines and other machines, and often little biotic sound. Soundscapes dominated by anthropogenic sounds have been linked to poor mental health in people, whereas the opposite has been found for natural sounds like birdsong or forest soundscapes.

Trump claims that the institution has fallen into the hands of Marxist radicals. A stroll through the exhibitions suggests otherwise.

August 20, 2026

The Immokalee Statue of Liberty in “Many Voices, One Nation,” at the National Museum of American History.Photograph by Lawren Simmons

Earlier this month, when I visited the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History (N.M.A.H.), President Trump’s signage warning of its “ideological capture” had yet to be installed. National Guardsmen marched in the paralyzing heat, which, along with the shadows cast by a revolving sculpture in the courtyard, suggested the eerie calm before the gunfight in a Western. Finally, the silence was broken by laughter—a group of volunteers from Citizen Historians for the Smithsonian, who’d advised me, via text, to look out for “4 old white ladies 🧓🏼🧑🏼‍🦳🧓🏼🧑🏼‍🦳”

“I just think what’s going on is a false narrative,” Deborah Greenbush, a D.C. tour guide who’s taken countless visitors through the museum, said. “I have never once had any adult or youngster express the feeling that what they saw made them feel bad. If it’s factual and actual, we should talk about it.” Next to her were Cindy Stevens, a former public-housing administrator, and Pege Gilgannon, a former photojournalist, who wore a shirt emblazoned with the words “Free D.C.” (She frequently volunteers for the D.C.-statehood movement.) Leading the group was Patti Curtis, a STEM adviser at the Department of Education, who retired just before its DOGE-driven evisceration. “They eliminated the entire research department,” she said. “I’m grateful that the Smithsonian isn’t just rolling over like some of our federal agencies.”

The four women are neighbors, and belong to a nonprofit community for seniors. “It’s your second family,” Gilgannon explained. “So you don’t just sit there playing mah-jongg.” Last summer, Curtis persuaded them to join Citizen Historians, a grassroots effort to monitor Smithsonian exhibitions for political interference. She’d heard about the group from one of its founders, James Millward, a central-Asia scholar at Georgetown. “He said, ‘I’ve taught in China and seen history erased, and I don’t want it to happen here.’ ” Not long before, Trump had pressured the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, to resign, in part because his official portrait’s wall text mentioned his two impeachments. Curtis organized forty volunteers to photograph its collections; altogether, more than seven hundred people have participated in Citizen Historian campaigns.

Trump’s anti-Smithsonian crusade began in March, 2025, with an executive order called “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” A declaration of war against a “revisionist movement” that saw America as “irredeemably flawed,” the order called for the removal of “improper ideology” from the Smithsonian’s twenty-one museums, and threatened to slash the institution’s funding if it didn’t comply. Soon, there were panicked reports—later debunked—that artifacts from slavery and the civil-rights movement had been quietly removed.

For a year, though, the Smithsonian has been spared, in part because of its semi-independent status. It’s governed by a seventeen-member Board of Regents, which includes the Vice-President, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, six federal lawmakers, and nine congressionally appointed members of the general public. The institution’s secretary, Lonnie G. Bunch III, has defended its integrity, but also shrewdly avoided provocative shows of resistance. Last August, he reportedly charmed Trump over lunch at the White House, and by the start of this summer’s Semiquincentennial celebrations, it was almost possible to believe that the Administration had moved on. Then, on July 4th, the White House Domestic Policy Council published a report called “Saving America’s Story,” which alleges that the N.M.A.H. has been hijacked by a cohort of radical activists. Shortly thereafter, Trump ordered the National Park Service to install warning signs outside the museum, whose director, Anthea Hartig, was summoned to testify on Capitol Hill.

“I was disturbed to hear about the quetzal,” Morgan Griffith, a congressman from Virginia, told Hartig, alluding to the suspiciously foreign bird feathers in a children’s show about money. (Quetzal feathers were once used as currency by the Aztecs and their trading partners in the American Southwest.) Nancy Mace, of South Carolina, called Hartig an ally of “queer pedophiles,” adducing, as evidence, a photo of RuPaul from an exhibition on American pop culture. Republicans also played a montage of Hartig making land acknowledgments, demanded to know why she’d once said that “loving America is very complicated,” and expressed outrage that no special exhibitions had been mounted about the Founding Fathers or the Declaration of Independence.

Democrats denounced the proceedings as a totalitarian show trial. Their star witness, the Pulitzer-winning historian David W. Blight, called the White House report “a declaration of political war on the historian’s profession,” and scoffed at accusations of left-wing revisionism. “All history is revision,” he said. “Would you prefer your doctors not to be revisionists?” Hartig, by contrast, was polite almost to the point of meekness, constrained by her role to “Sir”ing and “Ma’am”ing her inquisitors while affirming her commitment to a patriotism that was “not instructed but inspired.” She invited lawmakers to “walk the building with me” and “stand in front of the Star-Spangled Banner, in awe”—implying, not without reason, that many had never even visited the museum they were so determined to control.

If they did come, the Citizen Historians were determined to get there first. Curtis unfolded a map of the museum with eight galleries circled in hot pink. “We powwowed last night and realized we could hit four of them,” she explained. “Rather than split up, let’s go together and saturate.”

“Can anybody read that?” Gilgannon whispered, holding her phone up like a flashlight.

“Yeah, ‘Oh say can you see by the dawn’s early light,’ ” Curtis replied.

We were standing in the darkened chamber that houses the Star-Spangled Banner, whose tattered stripes were dimly visible behind glass. The flag was made by Mary Pickersgill, who sewed it with the help of her daughter, two nieces, and an “African-American indentured servant” named Grace Wisher. Curtis frowned. “Do we really think she was an ‘indentured servant’?” she asked, wondering if the label had originally read “slave.” Gilgannon sighed: “I hate how they put it in your head that you’re gonna get tricked.”

The White House report contends that N.M.A.H. has abandoned patriotism and erased the Founding Fathers in service of an “anti-white agenda” that seeks to “divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens.” But a quick search of the collections database revealed that nearly a hundred objects associated with George Washington and the Revolutionary War—including Washington’s uniform, his battle sword, and his dinner plates—were on display. From the Star-Spangled Banner, we made our way to Horatio Greenough’s 1841 sculpture of a shirtless, sword-bearing Washington, its caption explaining how the sculptor had captured his “highest and noblest virtues.” Greenbush, the tour guide, was amused by his neoclassically bare chest. “He would have been mortified, I’m sure.”

Behind Washington was “Many Voices, One Nation,” an exhibition about the struggle of disparate peoples to forge an American identity. A video collage showcasing America’s diversity played on loop near the entrance; Gilgannon, whose family comes from Belgium, said, “My mother’s in there.” The four women fanned out to photograph the objects on display: an Irish brooch, a Chinese-American shop sign, a collection of accessories abandoned by migrants in the Sonoran Desert. The report frames the show as “pro-illegal alien activism,” but hadn’t mentioned its Border Patrol uniform, whose caption praised the agent’s twenty-two years of service. Later, we gawked at the lavishly decorated 1963 Chevy Impala in “Corazón y vida,” another exhibit derided as a paean to “foreign” peoples—the Chicanos of Southern California, who started building “lowriders” with elaborate hydraulic systems in the nineteen-forties. “I think I’d be scared when it lifts up,” Curtis said, inspecting the undercarriage. “We went to see ‘The Odyssey’ in 4DX a few weeks ago and I was screaming!”

On the top floor was “American Democracy,” a sweeping exhibition about self-governance. Near the entrance was the desk where Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence. Farther in was paraphernalia from a quarter millennium of Presidential campaigns, including Trump’s. (There was even a MAGA hat.) The exhibition culminated in a display of protest signs. The report characterizes them as “almost all for various progressive causes,” and I quickly spotted slogans familiar from Black Lives Matter and the campaign for marriage equality. But equally prominent were “Secure Our Borders,” “Stop Abortion Now,” and projected footage from a Tea Party rally—all unmentioned. Gilgannon took a picture of one from the D.C.-statehood movement. “They practice and promote joy,” she explained. “At first, I thought, What’s this crazy woo-woo? But that’s what’s going to bond us together when we have to, like, fight the National Guard.”

There was plenty of joy in “Entertainment Nation,” a bright, busy, and noisily media-rich survey of American pop culture. Greeting visitors was a photo of the jazz trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie, a “cool, Cold Warrior” who used music to fight Communism. Nearby was the sheet music for Irving Berlin’s “God Bless America” and Dorothy’s ruby slippers from “The Wizard of Oz,” whose L.G.B.T.Q. affiliations somehow escaped Republican scrutiny. It took several minutes for Greenbush and me to find the exhibition’s most controversial inclusion—an animation sketch depicting Mickey Mouse’s début in “Steamboat Willie” (1928), whose caption links the character to “longstanding traditions of blackface minstrelsy.” For once, a Citizen Historian and the report were on the same side. “Who would even make that connection?” Greenbush scoffed. “Maybe I’m naïve, but I never would have thought that. And there were points where I did watch a lot of Mickey Mouse.”

During the hearings, Representative Brandon Gill, of Texas, asked Hartig a question precision-engineered to extract a disqualifying sound bite: “Is Mickey Mouse racist?” When she said no, Gill quoted the caption—and again, Hartig affirmed Mickey’s innocence. “You don’t think blackface minstrelsy is racist?” Gill asked, now genuinely confused. Hartig kept calm. “It’s not for me to determine what’s problematic,” she replied. “It’s for me to determine what’s accurate.”

It’s well established that the Mickey Mouse of “Steamboat Willie”—who wears white gloves and performs the minstrel standard “Turkey in the Straw” on a paddle steamer—has its roots in blackface, which was, for nearly a century, one of America’s most popular forms of entertainment. To Republican lawmakers, pointing this out is character assassination, an attempt to cancel poor Mickey and all who hold him dear. But if Representative Gill visited the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American Culture, he might be surprised to learn how many great Black entertainers—including Eubie Blake and Josephine Baker—share Mickey’s checkered beginnings, and with what impartial curiosity these are explored.

Our tour of “Entertainment Nation” concluded with a video installation called “What’s So Funny?” It juxtaposed racist moments in old films and cartoons—Judy Garland dancing in blackface, Bugs Bunny fighting the Indian Wars—with excerpts from the routines of nonwhite comedians such as Margaret Cho and Richard Pryor. We laughed and cringed by turns, our faces painted by the light from the projectors. The 1946 film “Song of the South” came on, and I could feel us all torn between humming along to “Zip-A-Dee-Do-Dah”—a song that my grandmother, a Black woman, loves enough that she once bought an alarm clock with the melody—and recoiling in shame from Uncle Remus’s toothy grin. “My grandfather was actually in minstrel shows,” Greenbush abruptly volunteered. And yet, there she was, protecting our messy common heritage from being wiped clean.

How did the Smithsonian commemorate American history in simpler times, before postmodernism, intersectionality, and the many other Hydra heads of “woke”? The museum’s Semiquincentennial exhibitions struck me as neutral enough. But in order to assess their patriotism objectively, I needed to see how the N.M.A.H. had marked the 1976 Bicentennial, when the museum, the Smithsonian, and the federal government were all helmed by white men.

To my surprise, there was nary an exhibition dedicated to a Founding Father. But there had been a monumental show called “The Nation of Nations,” whose subject was America’s diversity. It opened with a survey of Native cultures, tracing the country’s identity as a “nation of immigrants” to the first Siberians who crossed the Bering Strait. A display about Ellis Island—which played recordings in dozens of languages—celebrated modern immigration, while a re-created nineteenth-century classroom was used to explain the process of naturalization. An entire section dedicated to American prejudice included anti-Japanese signage and a Ku Klux Klan hood.

Curators seem not to have worried that this would divide the American people. In the exhibition catalogue, then secretary of the Smithsonian S. Dillon Ripley—a former intelligence officer who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by Ronald Reagan—describes America as “a place of turmoil among red men, white men, black men, and yellow men.” Yet no one hauled him before Congress to answer for stoking racial tensions, snubbing George Washington, or making America sad on her birthday. Today’s Smithsonian should be equally uncontroversial—and, without the Trump Administration’s propaganda, it probably would be.

The institution remains vulnerable. Republicans have proposed cutting its budget by more than ten per cent, and if they can fill the vacancies on its Board of Regents before the midterm elections, they may be able to fire Bunch. Yet there are also signs that the right’s revisionism panic might be petering out. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska recently came out in support of the Smithsonian, while the Second Lady, Usha Vance, even feels comfortable collaborating with it. In May, she led a story-time event at the N.M.A.H. in honor of Asian American and Pacific Islander Heritage Month—in other words, a D.E.I. event for children, at a museum that her party believes is full of “inappropriate sexual and ideological content.” (She read from “Masala Chai, Fast and Slow,” by Rajani LaRocca, who is also known for “Some of Us,” a book for early readers that celebrates immigrant citizenship.)

She’s not the only conservative who didn’t get the memo. The day after my visit to the N.M.A.H., I went to see “America’s Presidents” at the National Portrait Gallery, where I found a father and son snapping selfies in front of Trump’s glowering mien. “We wanted to have a last weekend together before he went off to college,” the man explained; earlier, they’d been to the National Air and Space Museum. The man proudly acknowledged supporting Trump, but seemed confused when I asked if he’d spotted anything “radical.” He recalled a caption about a “wealthy landowner back in the day” who’d enslaved Native Americans, which he wasn’t sure was relevant, but he wouldn’t go so far as to say that it ought to be removed. “I don’t know if it’s unpatriotic,” he said. “It’s all good and bad. It’s part of our history.” ♦

Julian Lucas, a staff writer, began contributing to The New Yorker in 2018.

title: Archaeologists Just Found a Fascinating Ancient Statue—Used as a Paving Stone in a Roman Road - Nautilus
content:
Imagine you’re such a prominent figure in the ancient Lydia kingdom that an artist sculpted a 7-foot statue of you. Only to later experience the ultimate indignity: Having that 7-foot sculpture of you broken up and recycled as paving slabs. 

Featured Video

That’s the story of a mysterious 2,500-year-old marble statue that archaeologists working at the Sardis site in what is now western Turkey recently discovered. The statue had been halved and placed face down along a major Roman colonnaded avenue. The Romans arrived in Sardis in 133 BCE, and apparently weren’t too reverential when it came to Lydian art and sculpture.

“It’s very rare to find such monumental sculptures of this period anywhere in the Mediterranean, and this exceptionally well-preserved, unique monument casts important new light on the major arts of Lydia, and on the Lydians’ ties to their own past,” Nicholas Cahill, field director of the Archaeological Exploration of Sardis (AES), said in a statement.

Read more: “How the Statutes of Easter Island Walked Into Place”

The figure is wearing a Greek chiton (a thin tunic) and a diagonally wrapped mantle, as well as a garment with horizontal folds that may be local but is difficult to place. With an upright stance and long, coiffed hair, the statue appears traditional in some respects. However, given the estimated date of construction of 470-450 BCE, the aesthetic doesn’t exactly fit the timeline.

“This sculptor knows about contemporary styles in Mediterranean and Anatolian sculpture, the interest in hands, and the structure of the face and so forth, and yet [the statue is] wearing clothes from 100 years earlier,” Cahill said. “I think they’re very clearly looking back to their own past.”

At the time the statue was sculpted, Sardis would have been ruled by the Achaemenid Persians and served as a major provincial center rather than an independent capital. Either way, it’s unclear who the statue is of, or what its significance might have originally been. One theory is that it was placed near the sanctuary of the native mother goddess Cybele, a significant spot in Sardis.

Part of the problem in understanding the statue’s meaning is that the Lydians left little behind in the way of written records, and much of what we know about them comes from Greek and Roman perspectives. It’s hard to deny, though, that at some point in time, it had quite the fall from grace.
