title: Sean Duffy in the Real World
author: @NewYorker
content:
I am a sucker for a travel show—if it involves people going to a place and doing a thing, count me in. My current favorites include the BBC’s “Race Across the World,” in which the scenery is usually the star—last season, sweeping shots of frozen mountain vistas had me itching to book a trip to Mongolia—and “Jet Lag: The Game,” a web series that a friend of a friend got me very, very into, in which three charming American nerds and a rotating guest player turn the world into the setting for a real-life board game, or similar. Here, the scenery is less the star than the hosts and the silly challenges they take on. In one recent season, the players had to “claim” as many adjacent U.S. states as possible by, for example, sculpting a butter animal (in Iowa), drinking at a bourbon distillery (in Kentucky), or doing time-zone trivia at a Margaritaville (in any state with a Margaritaville). It is, after all, five o’clock somewhere.

You can imagine my excitement, then, when I learned about a forthcoming YouTube offering called “The Great American Road Trip.” This one promised not only travel-show vibes but, perhaps, a sprinkling of reality TV, another guilty pleasure of mine. One of the hosts, Sean Duffy, appeared, back in 1997, on the sixth season of “The Real World,” the MTV staple in which bright young things from varied backgrounds moved in together, in this case in Boston; his memorable moments included calling one castmate a bitch and dry-humping another before gyrating with a pool cue. The new show’s other host, Rachel Campos, also appeared on a season of “The Real World”; later, she and Duffy met on a spinoff, “Road Rules” (more of the same, but on a road trip), got married, and had nine children. Campos-Duffy is now a host on Fox News; Duffy, who has hosted on Fox Business and served as a congressman from Wisconsin, is currently Donald Trump’s Transportation Secretary. Indeed, it was in this capacity that he launched “The Great American Road Trip,” with a promise to inspire other families to hit the road in honor of the country’s Semiquincentennial. “Our motto is ‘To love America is to see America,’ ” Duffy said, on Fox, in May. Campos-Duffy, sitting next to him, added that, in our “PornHub world,” the show would be “really wholesome, good family stuff.” A trailer promised as much—but also some drama.

By the time Duffy spoke about it on Fox, “The Great American Road Trip” was more or less in the can, and he said that episodes would drop in June, perhaps in time for the peak of the Semiquincentennial celebrations and summer travel season. But June brought no show, and neither did July. Meanwhile, controversy swirled around the initiative. Some critics attacked it as tone-deaf, given the war in Iran and the attendant, spiralling gas prices. (Rolling Stone calculated that a Duffy-style trip this summer might cost upward of a thousand dollars in fuel alone.) Others highlighted ethical concerns: the show was funded by a namesake nonprofit that cut sponsorship deals with various major companies—the aerospace giant Boeing, the construction provider CRH, the autonomous-driving service Waymo—that fall within Duffy’s regulatory purview. The Transportation Department insisted that this was all above board, claiming, among other things, that the road trip was official business and that Duffy had folded in relevant work meetings. After the trailer met with a withering reaction, Duffy took aim at a “radical, miserable left” that, he said, didn’t like what he was doing because “it’s too wholesome. It’s too patriotic. It’s too joyful.” During a contentious hearing before the Senate Appropriations Committee, Patty Murray, a Democrat from Washington, suggested that the whole endeavor stank. Duffy shot back, “Don’t you want to celebrate America? Let’s celebrate this country. It’s our birthday.”

On Wednesday, “The Great American Road Trip” finally landed on YouTube, in six episodes of a half hour or so each. (Technically, it should have been called “The Great American Road Trips”; as officials were keen to point out, it was filmed in installments over a period of months.) At long last, it was time to tune out the naysayers and joy haters, and judge the show on the only terms that matter for a product of the Trump Administration: whether or not it’s good TV.

During Trump’s first term, in particular, the President couldn’t pass a bowel movement without pundits declaring it “made for TV.” More often than not, I found this unbearably annoying—part of a persistent media inclination to grade the optics of the things that Trump did rather than, well, the things that Trump did. But I also felt annoyance at critics who seemed to see any mention of TV in politics as tantamount to dumbing down. TV, after all, can be very good!

Embarking on “The Great American Road Trip,” I quickly started to fear that it was not very good. The first episode—a trip to see Trump at the White House, then on to Philadelphia to learn about the Liberty Bell, meet a Benjamin Franklin impersonator, and race up the “Rocky” steps—has the feel of a promotional video that one might watch in the back of a cab. Patrick—one of the Duffys’ kids, a few of whom have clearly inherited their parents’ screen chops and brightened up the show considerably—matched my energy when a producer asked if he found it cool to visit the White House, and he replied that “it’s kind of boring, because you’re just sitting there watching your parents talk.” (“What’s so good about having cheese and steak?” Patrick asks later. “You can make that at home.”)

If Episode 1 put me to sleep, Episode 2 quickly jolted me awake. Before the Duffys even leave for their destination—Boston, this time—we learn that their daughter Paloma is applying to colleges, including Harvard, which, she says, would be hard to turn down. “Well, me and Mom can say no,” Duffy replies. Cue tense music and a disquisition on the importance of Catholicism to Duffy père and mère, who are concerned that Harvard has perfected how to take “good young girls” and “corrupt their minds.” Paloma doesn’t think that this is very open-minded, and the argument continues in the car. Eventually, both are parked—Duffy has taken the kids to see the firehouse that he once inhabited on “The Real World,” where they are welcomed in by Montana, the castmate he dry-humped. But the college plot soon recommences, and the Duffys eventually speak with a Harvard chaplain who, to some extent, is able to allay their anxieties about brainwashing. (“There is a refuge, it appears, in the Catholic Church” at Harvard, Duffy reflects. Campos-Duffy admits, “I didn’t wanna like the situation as much as I did.”) By this point, I was getting a little worried about the separation of church and state. Then I remembered, with relief, that the series was funded by corporate sponsors.

There is more drama in Episode 3 (Wyoming and Montana—the state, not the castmate): the Duffys’ eldest daughter, Evita, and her husband, Michael, who has amazing eyebrows and is currently vying for Duffy’s old congressional seat, invite an ultrasound technician to their cabin to find out the sex of their unborn child; meanwhile, Patrick has to go to the hospital after collapsing with visibly agonizing stomach pain that doctors think might be appendicitis. Happily, it turns out to be constipation, much to the amusement of the rest of the family. (“I don’t want to embarrass him,” one of his sisters says, long after that horse had bolted.) The remaining episodes—a trip to Charleston, with a detour to a Boeing plant; a trip to Texas, with a detour to a CRH subsidiary; a trip to Arizona, with a ride in a Waymo—mostly settle back into the tedium of Episode 1. Perhaps most upsetting for me, the show, as a whole, never seems to figure out whether it is primarily travel or reality, or whether the scenery or the people should be the star. The creators could have done more to bring out the gorgeous landscapes that the Duffys visited; they could, at least, have fed us some dumb challenges, with alcohol or not. Ultimately, I came away with no idea who the show is supposed to be for, although, if its paltry early view count is any guide, the answer might be “no one.”

A few months ago, in anticipation of the show’s release, I watched some old episodes of “The Real World” to get in the spirit. They were extremely dated. They were also vastly more interesting than “The Great American Road Trip” would prove to be. Duffy, for his part, came across as a real jerk at times, but surprisingly charming at others, with a half-nerd, half-jock mien—sweepy hair, big glasses, a megawatt smile—that put me in mind of a Wisconsin Sam Seaborn. (Call it “The Midwest Wing.”) According to the Times, Duffy told his “Real World” castmates that he aspired to be President one day, and “The Great American Road Trip” certainly had me wondering whether the point was to promote American travel or Duffy himself. For the record, Duffy has strongly disclaimed any interest in the White House, which is, after all, just a bunch of boring grownups talking. His show—in which he does beautiful family things with his beautiful family—does feel like a shop window, though. And, even if it isn’t, it’s an interesting thought experiment to consider whether, in this media moment, it would work as one.

It’s tempting to look at Duffy’s political ascent—and Trump’s, of course—and reflect on the surprising cultural sticking power of turn-of-the-millennium-style reality TV. And so, I will. The Trump Presidency likely wouldn’t have been possible without “The Apprentice.” Duffy’s rise has been less meteoric, but his launchpad, if anything, was an even purer distillation of the genre; as my colleague Emily Nussbaum has written, “The Real World” pioneered many of reality TV’s modern tropes—the cast of strangers, the apartment as set, the confessional interviews—and cultivated a viewership that no longer saw reality TV as a “crummy stopgap” for scripted fare but the thing to watch. When I revisited the show earlier this summer, it seemed a particularly propitious moment to assert the ongoing influence of reality TV, not least in politics. Spencer Pratt, the villain from “The Hills,” was running for mayor of Los Angeles, depicting the city as a hellhole and attracting reams of media coverage. Luke Gulbranson (“Summer House”) was running for a (year-round) U.S. House seat in Minnesota. Mark Moran (“FBoy Island”) was running for Senate in Virginia.

The moment no longer seems so propitious. Moran dropped out; Gulbranson lost, as, more significantly, did Pratt, occasioning some hand-wringing about whether his supposed surge had ever been real to begin with. (In fairness, almost nothing is more reality-TV than that.) More broadly, the genre’s future, at least as conventional TV, is in doubt, in this era of social media, podcasts, and YouTube. And yet, arguably, this array has made everything into reality TV and given everyone the tools to be a star; certainly, the genre’s codes—chiefly, its obsessions with conflict and with evaluating people’s authenticity—are baked into our modern media culture. Perhaps the most reality-TV moment of the past week came when the Georgia senator Jon Ossoff mocked Trump for flying around on his plane with “Natalie,” a winking reference to a young aide who is known for her particularly obsequious devotion to the President—and as the “human printer,” because she follows him around feeding him digital content in hard-copy form. The footage was endlessly clipped and debated. Trump responded by likening Ossoff to Pee-wee Herman. The White House communications director called him “the biggest cuck loser in politics.” (Ossoff, not Herman.)

It was certainly the most reality-TV moment of the past week to involve a politician’s travel schedule. Ironically, given his impeccable credentials, Duffy’s show didn’t come close: to the extent that it trades in “authenticity,” it is of the performative, Americana-drenched variety that the word has come to signify in politics, despite bearing little relationship to what’s real; nor does the show serve up any conflict. (Aside from the Harvard row, anyway, and even that ends happily. Spoiler ahead! Paloma is pleased to be accepted to the University of Chicago.) Throughout his political career, Duffy has seemed ambivalent about his reality roots, at times dismissing them as irrelevant, and at others leaning in, as he does, explicitly, in the Boston episode of “The Great American Road Trip,” and, implicitly, in the show’s over-all orientation. He has pushed back on the idea that the show is reality TV, but not all that convincingly—you can take the star out of reality, but not reality out of the star. Maybe, if he’d more successfully kept his distance, he could just have made a great travel show—something less “Real World” and more “real world.”

Duffy, of course, might believe that this is exactly what he did. Touting the series on X, he wrote, “America isn’t something you can understand through a phone screen. You have to get out and see it.” This is fair. If his show makes a compelling case for anything, it’s less screen time. ♦

title: The Big Question: What's your video game happy place?
author: @eurogamer
content:
We all have our happy places: somewhere - real or otherwise - to escape, relax, and replenish away from the stresses of the modern world. Perhaps yours is in nature, lost in the reverie of a spirited hike up a windy hill, or sweatily squatting your cares away amid the pounding Daruda Sandstorms of your local gym. Perhaps your demands are simpler: the call of a good book and an escape into the realm of imagination, or the familiar celluloid embrace of a favourite film, or - as I finally drag this intro into relevance - the soothing rhythms of a beloved video game. And hopefully it's the last one, because that's what we're talking about today.

As you might have noticed, it's Optimism Week here on Eurogamer - a chance, at a time it isn't always easy to remember, to reflect on how special video games can be. And to celebrate the occasion, we're reviving The Big Question to tackle another topical talking point before wafting it lovingly over to you. And this time: what's your video game happy place?

Do you prefer to take solace in the cosy idylls of the farming life, sinking dreamily into the comforting mundanity of turnip whispering? Perhaps your gaming happy place is one of nostalgia, the warmth of a retro favourite of old. As it happens, I've already written about one of my own favourite happy places: the vast procedural universe of No Man's Sky, where I can amble serenely with the vaguest of purposes, tweak my infinitely expanding base, dip into its wonderfully kind community, or idly tinker with its latest toys. But I've got other happy places, far removed: harsher, crueller worlds to explore.

FromSoftware's Souls games might not be what you'd typically call relaxing, but their exquisitely forlorn spaces are so meticulously, completely realised, I find it hard not to get lost in it all. But more than that, they practically force you into a meditative state; demanding calm, cautiousness, and clear-headed focus if you're to survive their merciless worlds. Nobody ever beat Ornstein and Smough by being impatient, after all (but I'm now ready to be informed otherwise in the comments!) So they're my happy places, but what about the rest of the Eurogamer team? We've asked, they've answered, and then it's over to you!

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (N64, 3DS)

There's a very special house in Hyrule Castle Town. A house full of pots. Pots you can smash. The guard inside will never stop you from smashing them. You can smash, smash, smash away to your hearts delight. Leave the house only to return and all of the pots will be back in place. Slip into an nirvana of pot smashing. - Lottie

RuneScape (PC, Mac, iOS, Android)

I've celebrated a very special anniversary this year as 2026 marks my 20th year of playing RuneScape. Something I definitely didn't expect when I made my first account on an April afternoon many, many, many moons ago.

Sure I've taken a break - a month here, a month there whenever the new content hasn't interested me or I simply haven't had enough time - but I've always come back, because I simply love the world of Gielinor. Sometimes I log in, not to play the game, but to simply go for a walk - be it the farmlands of Misthalin or the mountains of the Fremennik Province. Whether it's RuneScape 3 or Old School RuneScape, I feel like part of me is tied to Gielinor and hearing the opening score as the game boots up feels like going home. - Lottie

Super Mario 64 (N64, DS, Switch)

While it was tempting to say that Silent Hill is my happy place (which, honestly, it kinda is), I figured I'd go for the next best thing that's slightly more cheery; Princess Peach's Castle in Super Mario 64. As one of the first games I remember playing, and one of the few games I revisit and replay regularly as an adult, returning to Peach's Castle feels like going home in a way. Whether I am racing Koopa through Bob-omb Battlefield or being jump-scared by the flying books in Big Boo's Haunt, everywhere (that isn't an underwater level) is a very happy place for me; full of nostalgia, Toads, and flying slide-kicks - which I could never pull off as a child, but do so with pride now. - Kelsey

Rollercoaster Tycoon Classic (PC)

The joyous screams of a working park, the clack-clack-clack of chains pulling a rollercoaster train to its peak, and the cha-ching of money rolling in as guests flood in. The premise is simple - make a working and profitable theme park - but how you do it (or even if you do it) is entirely up to you. Whether I'm making literal death traps, or malfunctioning rides, I never tire of it. After making my first basic park, I keep finding new challenges and new build methods to try. - Marie

Spyro Reignited Trilogy (PS4)

Pretty much every Spyro game is my happy place, and this edition contains three (hence why I've chosen it). It's where I turn whenever I need a game that is familiar, that I don't have to think too hard about, and it still fills the 'I need entertaining but I don't want it to be too difficult' gap in my library. Seeing the purple dragon race across my screen while charging sheep to get butterflies to feed Sparx, or using his flame to blast away Rhynocs and setting Gnasty Gnorcs undies on fire, or whatever else he may be doing, it's yet to become dull. I simply love this little purple dragon and being a part of his adventures, and away from the Reignited Trilogy, there are so many more. - Marie

Jak and Daxter: The Precursor Legacy (PS5)

It's a yearly tradition at this point. Hearing the opening titles, punching Lurkers, Daxter's sarcastic quips when you die, powering up with eco... I could go on and on but will leave it at this: it makes me happy! - Marie

Quake 3 (PC)

It's nice to feel good at something isn't it? And there's one Quake 3 map I'm confident I can say that about: Q3DM17, also known as The Longest Yard. It's the one with the jump pads on; the one with that perilous leap out to the solitary platform in the spacey distance where the railgun spawns. The sitting duck leap.

I'm confident about being good at that map for two reasons. One, because I've played it so many times - hundreds, possibly thousands of times - that I know where all of the spawn points are, such that I can fire rockets to these locations to arrive when someone spawns. And two, because once upon a time, we played Quake 3 in the Eurogamer office and I trounced everyone on that map - and there were some very competitive Quake players here!

But it's only that map: I'm useless at all of the others. And it's that map in particular because it was available in a free demo version of Quake 3 that was all I had access to when I was younger. When I want to feel good at shooters, I boot it back up. It never fails to cheer me up. - Bertie

Hades 2 (Switch 2)

This has become my current happy place game! I'm surprised because I wasn't that 'in' to Hades 1; I sort of glanced off of the surface of it. But this one, I'm all in on. I think a lot of it being a happy place game has to do with the circular design of Roguelite games. Their being designed to be replayable in hour-ish chunks means they're really snackable, such that I find them much more tempting to play again than using that hour to get into a new game. After all, I've already done all the heavy lifting - I know what I'm doing now.

But an equally large part of it has to do with the game being Hades 2. It's just such a generous package. It's like a pass the parcel game that never stops unwrapping; every time I play, there's something new to do. And the playing of the game itself is exquisite - the speed, the snap, the chewy theorising over builds. I've been dabbling in it all year and see no reason why that'll end any time soon - Bertie

Critical Role (web series)

Bending the rules a bit here but Critical Role constitutes a gaming thing and it's certainly become a happy place for me, so I motion for it to count.

A few years ago, I wouldn't have predicted I'd become a 'Critter' - I wouldn't have thought I'd watch countless four-hour episodes of people playing predominantly Dungeons & Dragons. But here we are. And I'm now so excited about the current series helmed by Brennan Lee Mulligan that I genuinely look forward to a new episode more than maybe any other TV show.

There's lots I love about it - admiring actors' deep character work and their improvisational cool-heads to create stories on the spot; the laughs; the sense of community; the mutual support; the inclusivity - but something I come back to time and time again is just the presentation of the thing. One camera angle, mostly, and a relaxed, storytelling atmosphere. It makes for a refreshingly calming thing to watch in a world of strobe-like hyper-cut TV shows. I love it - Bertie

Lost Odyssey (Xbox 360)

This was the first RPG I believe I ever played, and you really can't beat your first right? The story was perhaps too good for my teenage brain, but something about the world, about the music, captured me. Like many others my age I was playing Halo and Call of Duty: Black Ops, but my heart was stuck with Kaim and the gang.

I remember swapping out the four discs on my Xbox 360 back in the day, and being genuinely unpleasable when the disc tray on my console broke. It kept me from my favourite game (and Dead Space 2, another honourable mention I'll sneak in here). I had to use a screwdriver to pry it open, which only worked for so long. The good ol' days.

This game is truly beautiful, and I still on occasion go back to revisit this classic. It pulls at your heartstrings, it's got some lovingly-crafted prose threaded throughout, and on top of all that it's got a killer turn-based RPG system under the hood. Well worth playing if you haven't had the chance - Connor

Guild Wars 2 (PC)

Gosh, this really is probably my favourite MMO of all time. It was a fierce competition between this, Maple Story, Old School RuneScape, and Classic World of Warcraft for a while but I think I'm landing on this one. The world is so beautiful, the gameplay so fun. I think I could play this game for another five years and be happy throughout.

It's just, there's so much to do and it all feels meaningful. I love collecting an achievement here and there, and filling out the wardrobe. I love trying out new weapons and seeing how they play. The story is good, the players are kind. It's a genuine masterclass of MMO design and I'm happy it's still popular even now. - Connor

Too Human (Xbox 360)

This game isn't one of the best. But it was there at just the right point in my life. Everyone I believe has a game they know isn't amazing but has a place close to their heart. I think some of the higher-end armour and weapons looked cool - I can't believe this was meant to be part of a trilogy. I wonder what Dennis Dyack is doing today. - Connor

Football Manager (PC)

One of the things that makes Football Manager feel like something of a safe space to me is the fact it doesn't really feel like a video game. There are a million ways to play this game but to me it's a game of optimisation. The absolute most efficient spend in a transfer window, and most optimal plan for upgrading a team over time (top tip: replace the weakest starting player with the strongest signing each window for the maximum average gain.)

It's where I can motivate a team perfectly. Where I can replay a conversation that didn't go well (don't judge me - in real life you can call people up and apologise!). Where I can formulate and execute my plan exactly. Or almost exactly, as players are ultimately outside your control. And that's what it's really about, for me: a place to retreat to where the world makes sense, where doing things the right way is rewarded, where I can identify problems with the world and then actually solve them.A power fantasy of its own. - Chris

FTL: Faster Than Light (PC, iOS)

I have a lot of happy places, if I'm honest. After Football Manager I could've put a childhood game here. A classic Pokémon game with a bit of modern tidying-up - a HeartGold or FireRed maybe - or Crash Team Racing, or Dawn of War. Pretend I wrote lots about those as well. But there is just something about FTL that even now, after years of writing about it, I struggle to truly put down. Maybe it's the isolation. There's something to the distance in FTL, the spaces between sectors, jumps, your ship and the others. The pauses between the battles where you just hang there, the chaos suddenly silent and your crew just happily at their stations, engines slowly coming back online. This is my meditative silence, just making decisions and looking after my little guys and inevitably crumbling when it gets too tough, and then going again for another silent ramble through the stars. - Chris

So that's the Big Question, and that's our gaming happy places... now it's over to you!

title: Entropy, a deliciously miserable Final Fantasy-esque RPG where your party members can permanently die, is now out in early access
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
It's not XCOMplicated

I was already aware of Entropy before Edwin called it a game that looked like a PS1 game fished from a toilet, primarily thanks to the stellar work developer Lovely Hellplace carried out in their previous game Dread Delusion, but I'm sure that would have hooked me in conceptually just as easily. And now you can dive into this turn-based, post-apocalyptic RPG yourself, as it's launched into early access.

The world of Entropy is a miserable one. There was no single thing that caused the pseudo end of the world, just the passage of time and "the inexplicable infertility of the world." At the point in time you start the game, very few humans remain, and you are putting on a theatre performance (for we must continue to make art even at the end). This is quickly ruined by the arrival of demons, forcing you to defend yourself before setting out towards hell itself.

𝔉𝔯𝔬𝔪 𝔱𝔥𝔢 𝔪𝔞𝔨𝔢𝔯𝔰 𝔬𝔣 𝔇𝔯𝔢𝔞𝔡 𝔇𝔢𝔩𝔲𝔰𝔦𝔬𝔫... 𝕰𝖓𝖙𝖗𝖔𝖕𝖞 is OUT NOW in Early Access!!! ⚔️Tactical Combat! 💀Soulslike Mechanics! 💬Narrative Conundrums! 🌎3D World Map! fr, the team have poured their hearts and souls into this one & I'm so proud of what we've achieved❤️ store.steampowered.com/app/3940340/...

[image or embed]

— James Wragg (@lovelyhellplace.bsky.social) August 18, 2026 at 4:37 PM

Apart from drawing a comparison to the contents of a toilet, Edwin did also pull on Final Fantasy when describing the game, to give you a frame of reference for what you should expect in terms of the turn-based elements. There's an overworld to explore too, harkening back to those Final Fantasies of old. Where it differs is the fact that your not-so-merry band of mercenaries can permanently die in an XCOMian manner, putting great pressure on your playing to ensure that doesn't happen. As I've told you, this is a miserable world, and these mercs are no different.

In terms of what you can expect from this early access release, the entire first act of the game, which the Steam page explains is roughly a quarter of the full thing. That includes "two towns, three dungeons, and numerous smaller locations and challenges - with plenty of characters, weapons, armours and spells to acquire." So, sounds like you've got enough to get stuck in with! It should be in early access for about a year, with two more acts to come. If you're uncertain that it'll be your cup of bogwater, you can try out a demo still, or alternatively you can just pick it up on Steam.

title: Just in case you thought it wasn't going to be a huge game, Square Enix confirms Final Fantasy Resonance is getting a 120-song original soundtrack.
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
Lightning strikes twice.

Earlier this year, Square Enix announced that we'll be getting our first HD-2D Final Fantasy game in October this year, and it's based on the now-shuttered mobile title Brave Exvius.

We've had a few trailers from the game since, and it's certainly looking like it's going to be a massive tite. Now, Square Enix has announced the game is getting a proper soundtrack treatment, with the Final Fantasy Resonance Original Soundtrack will releasing a week after the game comes out (on 28th October), with an OST that spreads over four CDs and 120 tracks.

Watch on YouTube

The soundtrack features music produced by Noriyasu Agematsu, who has created an additional 33 tracks for this soundtrack to complement the 87 that were already released for both Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, and War of the Visions: Final Fantasy Brave Exvius.

There are some absolutely amazing names for some of the tracks (which you can see here), including the likes of "Leviathanomachy", "Wickedness Afoot", "A Bloom in the Gloom of Shadows", "Break the Limit!", "He Who Shoulders Umbral Darkness" and "Overcome the Menace". If you're curious about how the size of this OST compares to other Final Fantasy games, the digital version of Final Fantasy 10 includes 89 tracks, Final Fantasy 7 has 85, and Final Fantasy 8 has 73. So you can expect a lot of music in Resonance, then.

If you're keen on owning a physical version of the OST, you can pre-oreder the CD here in the EU, here in North America, and here in Japan.

I'm pretty excited for Final Fantasy Resonance; the general pitch of the game from Square Enix itself is: 'What if Final Fantasy had continued to push the limits of pixel art?' - a question many people have been asking since the series moved to 3D for its mainline games with Final Fantasy 7 in 1997. With games like Octopath Traveler and Triangle Strategy demonstrating Square Enix's skill with the new-fangled HD-2D genre - and having decent success with wrangling decent single-player games out of its mobile gacha experiments - Resonance is a bit of a no-brainer for the publisher. Let's just hope the game can stick the landing and live up to how good all the trailers have been, to date.
